Clarity.justification: The paper is well-structured with clear sections (Introduction, Related Work, Methodology, Experimental Setup, Results, Discussion, Conclusion), logical flow, explicit hypotheses (h-e1 to h-m3), tables summarizing metrics, and code snippets for each validation layer. Ideas such as the three-layer architecture (schema + pattern + compositional contracts) and constraint formalizations (C1-C4) are articulated precisely. Minor deductions for repetitive phrasing in the Discussion and excessive length in sections 3 and 6.

Novelty.justification: The paper applies Design-by-Contract principles (preconditions, postconditions, invariants) to research pipeline phase transitions, which is a modest extension of existing formal methods work (Eiffel, icontract) and multi-level validation (Great Expectations). No new theoretical contributions or algorithms are introduced. The core claim of 100% downstream failure reduction is demonstrated only on placeholder hypothesis content with typed interfaces, and the paper explicitly states that external validity to substantive research remains unproven.

Soundness.justification: All experimental results are obtained on a 100-case placeholder hypothesis corpus and a 25-case adversarial test suite with minimal substantive content; the paper repeatedly acknowledges that 'external validity to substantive research content remains unproven' and 'generalization to production workflows with complex semantic dependencies' is deferred. The provided code file contains only a single JSON result object for h-m2 with no actual implementation or real data. The schema-only baseline deliberately excludes field validators, creating an artificially large expressiveness gap. No real ML research content, datasets, or production pipelines are evaluated.

Significance.justification: The paper addresses automated research pipeline validation with feasibility constraints (no synthetic data, no human evaluation, standard datasets only) but has no connection to the workshop topic of bidirectional Human-AI alignment, human values, RLHF, societal norms, or any of the listed scopes (Specification, Methods, Evaluation, Deployment, Societal Impact). The claimed contributions (three-layer contracts, 100% failure reduction on placeholders) do not advance the field of AI alignment or address any workshop challenge.

strengths: Clear presentation of the three-layer validation architecture and constraint formalizations
Explicit acknowledgment of limitations regarding placeholder content and external validity
weaknesses: Complete mismatch with workshop scope on bidirectional Human-AI alignment
All empirical claims rest on placeholder data with explicitly unproven external validity; results are not real
